title: 1 Kings 3:1–5
context: With the kingdom secured at the end of chapter 2, the narrator opens Solomon’s reign with a mixed picture. Solomon makes a marriage alliance with Pharaoh, builds in Jerusalem, and loves the LORD, yet he and the people still worship at high places because the temple has not been built. The passage then moves to Gibeon, the “great high place,” where Solomon offers a thousand burnt offerings and the LORD appears to him in a dream. The Pharaoh is not named, and identifications proposed by historians remain uncertain. Both traditions read these verses as a sober introduction: genuine devotion stands alongside compromises that the later story will not ignore, and the initiative in the dream belongs entirely to God.

verses.text: Solomon made a marriage alliance with Pharaoh king of Egypt. He took Pharaoh’s daughter and brought her into David’s city until he had finished building his own house, the LORD’s house, and the wall around Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that the narrator places Solomon’s marriage alliance with Pharaoh at the head of his reign without comment, and many hear in it an early hint of the foreign marriages that later turn his heart away (1 Kings 11:1–8; compare Deuteronomy 17:17). Solomon’s choices are presented as real decisions whose consequences will unfold over time.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the alliance as politically shrewd but spiritually ambiguous, setting the stage for the later account of Solomon’s many wives. Both traditions agree that the verse also shows God’s purposes advancing, since David’s son is building the LORD’s house and Jerusalem’s wall, while the seeds of later failure are already visible in the same sentence.

verses.text: However, the people sacrificed in the high places, because there was not yet a house built for the LORD’s name.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers observe that the narrator explains rather than condemns the people’s worship at the high places, tying it to the fact that no house had yet been built for the LORD’s name. The verse acknowledges a transitional period in which sincere worshipers acted within real limitations, and it anticipates the temple as the place God would choose (Deuteronomy 12:5–14).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same explanation and stress that the verse looks forward to the temple as the divinely appointed center of worship. Both traditions recognize that the narrator’s “However” signals some unease about the high places, even in this early period, and that how far such worship was tolerated before the temple is a question interpreters weigh carefully rather than settle quickly.

verses.text: Solomon loved the LORD, walking in the statutes of David his father, except that he sacrificed and burned incense in the high places.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers highlight that Solomon “loved the LORD,” a statement of genuine covenant devotion, and that he walked in the statutes of David his father. The qualification that follows shows that love for God and imperfect obedience can coexist, and the narrative invites readers to see a heart that must keep choosing faithfulness as the story continues.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also value the plain statement that Solomon loved the LORD and see it as a fruit of the covenant God made with David’s house. Both traditions agree that the “except” is not a throwaway line; it honestly records a flaw in Solomon’s worship that the books of Kings will repeatedly measure against the standard of faithful worship at the place the LORD chooses.

verses.text: The king went to Gibeon to sacrifice there, for that was the great high place. Solomon offered a thousand burnt offerings on that altar.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Solomon’s thousand burnt offerings at Gibeon express extravagant devotion at the start of his reign. Gibeon is called the great high place, and the Chronicler adds that the tent of meeting and the bronze altar were there (2 Chronicles 1:3–6), which many readers take as a reason this worship was regarded as more acceptable than at other high places, though the matter is debated.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers similarly note the scale of Solomon’s offerings and the significance of Gibeon as a site connected to Israel’s earlier worship. Both traditions see the offerings as a sincere act of worship that God graciously meets, while recognizing that interpreters differ on how fully the narrator approves of Gibeon’s status as a high place before the temple was built.

verses.text: In Gibeon, the LORD appeared to Solomon in a dream by night; and God said, “Ask for what I should give you.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers emphasize that the LORD takes the initiative, appearing to Solomon in a dream and inviting him to ask. The open invitation treats Solomon as a genuine partner in the relationship, whose request will reveal the priorities of his heart, and God’s response in the following verses shows that what Solomon chooses to ask for truly matters.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress the sheer graciousness of the invitation: the LORD appears and offers a gift before Solomon has done anything to secure it. Both traditions agree that the dream is an act of divine kindness to David’s son, that God is the giver throughout the scene, and that Solomon’s answer will be shaped by what he understands about God’s faithfulness to his father.
